plans.name: Standing up a programme from nothing
plans.when: Nobody owns AI governance yet, or someone has just been handed the brief.
plans.assumes: You can get a decision-maker in a room, and you have a few days a week.

phases.goal: Know what you have and get a mandate.

steps.do: Baseline honestly with the maturity assessment
steps.title: Maturity Assessment
steps.evidence: A dated baseline score with evidence against each dimension.
steps.note: Score what is true, not what is intended. This number is the benchmark every later improvement is measured against.

steps.do: Run a discovery sweep and build the AI inventory
steps.title: AI System Inventory
steps.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
steps.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.
steps.note: Ask teams, then check SaaS release notes, expenses, and SSO logs. Budget for finding two to three times what people report.

steps.do: Screen everything for prohibited practices
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.
steps.note: Prohibited practices have been in force since February 2025. If you find one, this becomes urgent and everything else waits.

steps.do: Get a written mandate
steps.title: Governance Charter
steps.evidence: A board-approved mandate naming the sponsor and the authority to halt.
steps.note: Two pages. The clauses that matter are the authority to halt a system and a named executive sponsor.

done: You can name every AI system in the organisation
Someone senior has signed something saying you own this
You know whether you have a prohibited-practice problem

phases.goal: Put the rules and the decision-making in place.

steps.do: Publish the acceptable AI use policy
steps.title: Acceptable AI Use Policy
steps.evidence: A one-page policy staff have attested to, with an approved-tool list.
steps.note: The highest-value document in the kit for the effort. Staff are already using AI; this is catching up, not getting ahead.

steps.do: Classify every system by risk tier
steps.title: AI System Inventory
steps.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
steps.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.
steps.note: Record the rationale, not just the label.

steps.do: Stand up the committee and agree decision rights
steps.title: Committee Charter (Terms of Reference)
steps.evidence: Terms of reference with quorum and the right to halt a system.
steps.note: Settle quorum and who can halt a live system before the first meeting, not during the first incident.

steps.do: Agree the RACI
steps.title: RACI Matrix
steps.owner: Governance lead, agreed in a room
steps.evidence: One accountable party per activity, confirmed by the people named.
steps.note: Do it in a room with the actual people. The argument is the point.

done: Staff know what they may and may not do
Every system has a tier and a named owner
A forum exists that can actually decide things

phases.goal: Assess the risky ones and make it visible.

steps.do: Assess your high-risk systems properly
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.
steps.note: Test subgroups, not just aggregate accuracy, and check whether human oversight is real by looking at the override rate.

steps.do: Open the risk register and incident log
steps.title: Risk Register
steps.evidence: Risks written as cause-event-consequence, each with an owner.
steps.note: You need the incident route defined before the first incident, not during it.

steps.do: Take the first board pack
steps.title: Board Pack Template
steps.evidence: A pack the board reads, with the decisions being sought stated.
steps.note: Take the assessment and export the Board view — it writes most of it. Lead with what you need, not what you did.

done: High-risk systems have completed assessments with owners
The board has seen a posture and been asked for something
You have a repeatable cycle rather than a project

plans.name: AI is landing faster than governance
plans.when: The business is shipping AI and you are trying to get in front of it.
plans.assumes: Governance exists in some form; the problem is pace, not mandate.

steps.do: Publish the acceptable AI use policy immediately
steps.title: Acceptable AI Use Policy
steps.evidence: A one-page policy staff have attested to, with an approved-tool list.
steps.note: Ship a one-page version this week. A perfect policy next quarter is worth less than a usable one now.

steps.do: Build the inventory, starting with what is already live
steps.title: AI System Inventory
steps.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
steps.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.
steps.note: Live systems first; pipeline second.

steps.do: Add an intake gate so new systems get screened
steps.title: AI Development & Deployment Standard
steps.evidence: Lifecycle gates enforced in the pipeline, producing evidence.
steps.note: One gate at intake beats a review at launch, because at launch the money is already spent.

done: Nothing new goes live unscreened
You know what is already running

phases.goal: Assess what is live and govern what is coming.

steps.do: Run the EU AI Act readiness checklist
steps.title: EU AI Act — 25-point readiness checklist
steps.evidence: A dated position against all 25 points.

steps.do: Classify and assess high-risk systems
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.

steps.do: Bring vendor AI under control
steps.title: Third-Party AI Risk Policy
steps.evidence: An assessment on file for every critical AI vendor.
steps.note: Most of your exposure is AI switched on inside software you already bought. Start with the release notes.

done: Every live system has a tier
Vendor AI is assessed rather than assumed

steps.do: Document your material models
steps.title: Model Card / Model Risk Documentation
steps.evidence: Documentation covering intended use, limitations and subgroup results.

steps.do: Set up monitoring and the incident route
steps.title: Issue & Incident Log
steps.evidence: A defined route people can name, plus the log itself.

steps.do: Start reporting a small metric set
steps.title: KPI / KRI Dashboard
steps.evidence: A stable metric set with trend over at least three periods.
steps.note: Six metrics held stable beats twenty that change every quarter — trend is the point.

done: Governance runs at the pace of delivery rather than behind it

plans.name: A regulator or board is asking questions
plans.when: Something has prompted scrutiny and you need a defensible answer soon.
plans.assumes: You have limited time and need evidence, not documents.

phases.goal: Be able to answer the question.

steps.do: Take the assessment, Regulator view, and export it
steps.title: EU AI Act — 25-point readiness checklist
steps.evidence: A dated position against all 25 points.
steps.note: The export lists what evidence each obligation needs. Assemble against that list rather than guessing what they will ask for.

steps.do: Produce the inventory, however imperfect
steps.title: AI System Inventory
steps.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
steps.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.
steps.note: "We are still completing it, here is what we have and when it will be finished" is a far better answer than silence.

steps.do: Assemble a board pack from what exists
steps.title: Board Pack Template
steps.evidence: A pack the board reads, with the decisions being sought stated.
steps.note: Be honest about the gaps. An amber pack with a plan lands better than a green one that unravels.

done: You can state your position with evidence behind it

phases.goal: Close the gaps that were exposed.

steps.do: Build the control library and assurance map
steps.title: Control Library & Assurance Map
steps.evidence: Obligations mapped to controls, each with an owner and evidence.
steps.note: The blank cells are the finding — obligations nobody is assuring.

steps.do: Formalise the risk register
steps.title: Risk Register
steps.evidence: Risks written as cause-event-consequence, each with an owner.

steps.do: Fix the highest-severity gaps from the assessment
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.

done: Every obligation has a control, an owner, and evidence

steps.do: Re-run the assessment and show the delta
steps.title: Maturity Assessment
steps.evidence: A dated baseline score with evidence against each dimension.
steps.note: Movement is more persuasive than any absolute score. Keep the first export so you can show the before.

steps.do: Report progress to the board
steps.title: Board Pack Template
steps.evidence: A pack the board reads, with the decisions being sought stated.

steps.do: Set the ongoing review cadence
steps.title: Committee Charter (Terms of Reference)
steps.evidence: Terms of reference with quorum and the right to halt a system.

done: Scrutiny has become a routine reporting cycle

plans.name: Small or flat organisation
plans.when: Fewer than ~150 people, no committee, no dedicated governance role, and this is somebody's third priority.
plans.assumes: Nothing. This path deliberately does not require a committee to exist.

phases.goal: The two things that actually reduce risk.

steps.do: List your AI systems in a spreadsheet
steps.title: AI System Inventory
steps.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
steps.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.
steps.note: Owner, source, tier, rationale. Four columns is enough. Do not buy a tool.

steps.do: Publish a one-page AI use policy
steps.title: Acceptable AI Use Policy
steps.evidence: A one-page policy staff have attested to, with an approved-tool list.
steps.note: Sections 2, 3 and 4 of the template only — the short version, approved tools, and what is never allowed.

steps.do: Check nothing is prohibited
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.
steps.note: The eight-item screen. This is the one check with no proportionality argument available.

done: You know what you run and staff know the rules

steps.do: Name one accountable person per system
steps.title: Roles & Responsibilities
steps.evidence: Named holders who know they hold the role.
steps.note: One person can hold several roles. The only split you must keep is that nobody assures their own work.

steps.do: Write down who can stop a system
steps.title: Decision Rights & Escalation
steps.evidence: A decision matrix tested against a real past decision.
steps.note: Two levels is enough: who decides day to day, and who they escalate to. Keep suspension distributed.

steps.do: Assess anything that affects people
steps.title: AI Risk Assessment
steps.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.
steps.note: Sections 1, 2 and 4 only — is it allowed, who could it hurt, who is watching. That fits on two pages.

done: Every system has a named human, and stopping one is possible

phases.goal: Enough evidence to answer a customer or auditor.

steps.do: Start an incident log, even if it is empty
steps.title: Issue & Incident Log
steps.evidence: A defined route people can name, plus the log itself.
steps.note: An empty log with a defined route beats no route. You need it before the first incident.

steps.do: Keep a short risk list
steps.title: Risk Register
steps.evidence: Risks written as cause-event-consequence, each with an owner.
steps.note: A 3x3 matrix and five risks you actually review.

steps.do: Do a half-day review every quarter
steps.title: Board Pack Template
steps.evidence: A pack the board reads, with the decisions being sought stated.
steps.note: A standing 45-minute item on an existing leadership meeting, with real minutes, beats a committee that quietly stops meeting.

done: You can evidence governance proportionate to your size
The cycle survives the person who set it up leaving
